conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a well-studied tool that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the first weeks and months after birth.

Nothing you share today goes beyond this room unless you or baby’s safety is at immediate risk, so please feel comfortable answering honestly. There are just ten questions about the past seven days; we’ll take them one at a time, and there are no right or wrong answers.

Ready to start? Here’s the first:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things—like a warm drink, a song on the radio, or your baby’s smile—or has that enjoyment slipped away?

Honestly? Most of the time those little things just feel kind of… flat. I can still smile when the baby grins at me, but even that happiness feels smaller than it used to, and it fades fast. A warm drink tastes fine, yet I don’t get that cozy feeling I remember. Same with music—I hear it, but it doesn’t lift me the way it did before she was born. Everything’s more muted, like I’m watching life through a foggy window.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, every now and then something small will make me crack a smile, but it feels forced. Mostly I just feel too tired or down to find things funny. Even when my partner tries to joke with me, I can’t seem to laugh the way I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. When I think about the week ahead—like meeting a friend for coffee or taking the baby to the park—I mostly feel “meh,” not excited. There are moments I hope things might feel fun again, but the actual looking-forward part just isn’t there right now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy and won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong as a mom. The other night she wouldn’t latch, and I sat there crying, telling myself I must be terrible at this. Even little stuff—like spilling a bottle or forgetting to bring a diaper—makes me feel like I’m failing her.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure she’s stopped breathing—so I have to put my finger under her nose to check. Or I’ll lie in bed replaying every little thing that could go wrong: what if I trip on the stairs, what if the dog knocks over the bassinet, what if I’m too asleep to hear her cry. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just circle and won’t quit.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week. Once, in the grocery store, my chest got tight and my hands felt shaky like something awful was about to happen—I left my cart and rushed back to the car just to breathe. And at home, when she’s napping, I’ll suddenly feel this wave of “what if I can’t protect her?” and my heart pounds. It comes out of nowhere and passes, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll start one chore, hear the baby cry, drop everything to soothe her, then look around at the mess and just feel paralyzed. Sometimes I sit on the couch with her asleep on me, afraid to move because as soon as I do, ten more things will need doing. I manage, but it’s like I’m always two steps behind and the pile keeps growing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t settle. I keep replaying everything I think I did wrong that day—did I burp her long enough, did I snap at my partner, am I already ruining her life? Some nights it takes me an hour or two to drift off, and then I jolt awake sure I heard her cry, even when she’s still asleep. It’s like my body’s tired but my mind keeps spinning.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time. I wake up with this heavy feeling in my chest, and it just kind of stays there. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but it’s wrapped in this sadness I can’t shake. Little things make me want to cry—like seeing another mom laughing with her kids or even a diaper commercial. I keep thinking I should feel grateful, and then I feel worse because I don’t.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple times this week. Yesterday I spilled some pumped milk and just sat on the kitchen floor sobbing; it felt like the worst thing in the world. And two nights ago, when she wouldn’t settle for almost an hour, the tears came while I rocked her. I try to keep quiet so she doesn’t see me upset, but the crying just sneaks up and takes over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s crossed my mind once or twice, just flashes—like “what if I just kept driving past the house and never came back,” or thinking maybe everyone would be better off without me. I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to die, but when I’m really overwhelmed the idea pops in for a second before I push it away.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels distant right now-how laughter, excitement, and even music seem muted or forced, and how a heavy sadness lingers from morning to night. You described daily <sym>worry</sym> that makes you check your baby's breathing, <sym>panic</sym> that sends you out of a store, and <sym>guilt</sym> that whispers you're failing her over spilled milk or a missed burp. Sleep is hard to find because your mind replays every perceived mistake, and tears arrive uninvited. Most of all, you feel overwhelmed and, at the worst moments, have fleeting thoughts that everyone might be better off without you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no spontaneous laughter, describes humor as forced, and inability to laugh as before, aligning with 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports minimal to no anticipatory enjoyment, describing a pervasive "meh" feeling and absence of looking-forward emotions, aligning with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('a lot') tied to multiple everyday infant-care situations, indicating the most severe endorsement.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive catastrophic worries without actual triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring "a few times this week" without obvious triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, paralysis, and inability to keep up, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive thoughts and racing mind causing prolonged sleep onset and fragmented sleep, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness 'most of the time,' persistent heavy feeling, frequent tearfulness, and inability to shake the mood, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear crying episodes this week triggered by minor stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse core symptoms: daily low mood and loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), pathologic self-blame, prominent anxiety and panic, middle/late insomnia, functional impairment, and passive suicidal ideation (Q10 ≥1). These findings meet <med>DSM-5</med> criteria when combined with clinician interview. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for full evaluation and safety plan
2. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Share these results with a trusted partner/friend who can stay with you until professional help is in place
4. Begin gentle daily routine: one small outdoor walk, balanced meals every 3-4 h, and 15 min rest when baby sleeps to reduce <sym>fatigue</sym>
5. Limit isolation-schedule one supportive phone call or visit each day; accept help with housework/meals
6. Consider referral to evidence-based therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression) and discussion of medication options compatible with breastfeeding if applicable
7. Follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
8. If panic symptoms surge, try slow breathing: inhale 4 s, exhale 6 s x 5 cycles and ground yourself by naming 5 things you can see/hear/feel
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed (maternal self-report, 0–48 hrs ago)  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1,2,8,9)  
- Pathologic guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Intrusive, excessive anxiety and panic episodes without clear precipitant (Q4,5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, difficulty completing daily tasks (Q6)  
- Initial insomnia with rumination; frequent nocturnal checking of infant (Q7)  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan or intent) (Q10)

Pattern  
Responses cluster in depressive (items 1,2,3,7,8,9) and anxiety (items 4,5) domains; functional impairment and safety concern present.

Risk flags  
- Daily crying spells  
- Sleep disruption tied to mood  
- Panic-type episodes  
- Passive self-harm thoughts  

Screening impression  
High-risk presentation consistent with probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; safety risk identified (passive SI). Recommend immediate formal psychiatric evaluation, suicide-risk assessment, and consideration of crisis/safety-planning resources.
